account:
Today’s unusual business seems to concern grain and bread supplies, although I do not yet know its extent or purpose. The secretary overheard the builder discussing a grain shortage and seeking the miller’s help, mentioning forty-six hay bales. That number and the circumstances remain unverified. The neighbour personally saw the baker give bread to the innkeeper yesterday; the innkeeper asked about spare wheat or hay, and freight told the neighbour they were seeking the miller about arrangements. These might be efforts to arrange supplies, but I have no direct confirmation of a shortage. The neighbour reports that the baker said yesterday’s bread arrangements went smoothly and that fresh bread was being baked today.

I went to the mill for my ten o’clock grain inspection, but did not locate the miller despite entering and calling out. The neighbour also got no answer at the mill earlier. I checked near the bakery without finding either the baker or miller. Townsfolk have repeated vague reports of a ‘bridge or port change’ at the bakery and a baker carrying a sack of bread. I have not witnessed any such change, and those reports do not explain what actually happened. A sack of bread alone is not evidence of wrongdoing.

The builder has also arranged an eighteen-hundred great-hall lighting inspection, confirmed with me, and intends to meet me shortly beforehand and accompany me inside. That is scheduled town business; I have no evidence connecting it to the grain arrangements. I am home for lunch now, with council letters at the office at thirteen hundred, tea with the neighbour at the east-bank cottage at fifteen hundred, and office time at sixteen-thirty before the inspection. I should keep these appointments and seek firsthand clarification of the supply arrangements rather than treat circulating reports as established facts.
